content:
Auto parts prices are climbing 10 to 20 percent in the border zone as high steel costs and U.S. tariff restrictions squeeze the industry — but a flood of cheap, low-quality parts is keeping the sticker shock hidden, according to Nuevo Laredo's chamber of commerce.

"El alto costo del acero y las restricciones arancelarias impuestas por Estados Unidos afectan directamente el precio de las refacciones en la zona fronteriza, con aumentos del 10 hasta un 20 por ciento," said Guillermo Cantú Salinas, vice president of Canaco in Nuevo Laredo.

The catch, Cantú said, is that low-priced, very low-quality parts arriving from China, Taiwan, and other Asian countries — brought in through intermediaries rather than directly — are holding overall prices down. Many new, unfamiliar brands have entered the market, and their prices do not reflect the increase. Good-quality metal parts, by contrast, have held their price because they carry the cost of parts from other origins.

What the industry data shows

According to data from the Industria Nacional de Autopartes (INA), the cost of auto parts in Mexico — and even more so in the border zone — has risen at least 10 percent this year. That increase is affecting the parts supply chain and slowing production momentum along Mexico's northern border.

Vehicle owners, squeezed by the broader economy, are trying to spend as little as possible on parts, Cantú said. But the difference between a cheap part and a quality one is not only the price — it is how long the part lasts. Brands from the United States, Canada, and Mexico are good quality, he said, and prices also shift with the peso-dollar exchange rate: when the dollar rises, demand for parts rises too.

Cantú's advice to vehicle owners: buy brand-name parts, with a good warranty.

Why it matters in Laredo

Many Laredo families buy parts across the border or have repairs done in Nuevo Laredo, where prices have long been lower. A part that costs less up front but fails sooner can end up costing more — in a second repair, a tow, or a breakdown on the highway. Shoppers comparing prices on both sides of the river should check the brand and the warranty, not just the price tag.
